questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the part of a README that most student projects skip, but that actually matters most to someone evaluating the code?
options: The license section
A "design decisions" section explaining why choices were made (e.g. why config is validated at startup, why errors are returned as Result<T>)
A list of every npm package version
A table of contents
questions.explain: The lesson calls out the "design decisions" section specifically — explaining the why behind choices — as the difference between "I followed a tutorial" and demonstrating real understanding.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how should you answer "what would you change for production?" about chain-reader in an interview?
options: Claim the project is already fully production-ready with no changes needed
Name specific, real follow-ups like retry-with-backoff for RPC calls, structured logging instead of console.log, and a fallback RPC provider
Say you would rewrite it in a different programming language entirely
Avoid answering because the capstone wasn't meant for production use
questions.explain: The lesson gives concrete, specific production follow-ups (retry logic, structured logging, provider fallback) as the kind of honest, credible answer to give.

questions.q: Which chapter does this lesson credit with applying TypeScript specifically to blockchain data and real libraries like ethers/viem?
options: Chapter 4 (TypeScript Fundamentals)
Chapter 6 (Node.js Basics)
Chapter 5 (TypeScript for Blockchain Development)
Chapter 1 (Programming Fundamentals Through JavaScript)
questions.explain: The course recap explicitly assigns Chapter 5 to applying TypeScript to blockchain data, ethers/viem, type-safe contract calls, project configuration, and recurring patterns.

questions.q: What is the next course in the Blockchain Engineer path after this one, according to the lesson's outro?
options: Blockchain Testing & DevOps
DeFi & Token Engineering
Blockchain Development
Blockchain Engineering Capstones
questions.explain: The lesson names "Blockchain Development" as the next course, where Ethereum, smart contracts, and Solidity begin — matching the Blockchain Engineer path's courseSlugs order (js-ts-blockchain, then blockchain).

questions.q: Why does the lesson suggest giving a specific, honest answer to "what was the hardest part?" rather than claiming nothing was difficult?
options: Because interviewers are required by law to ask this question
Because a real, specific answer (even something small, like getting tsconfig's target right for bigint literals) reads as more credible than claiming nothing was hard
Because every project must have at least one unsolved bug
Because this question has no bearing on how an interview goes
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states a real, honest, specific answer is more credible than a claim that nothing was difficult, using the tsconfig/bigint target issue from Lesson 29 as an example of a small but real difficulty.
